drills.q: Given a 2-second end-to-end latency target, build a budget across embedding, ANN search, reranking, and generation.
drills.a: A defensible split: ~75ms embedding, ~100ms ANN retrieval, ~250ms rerank (over ~top-100), ~75ms buffer, leaving ~1500ms (~75%) for generation, which dominates because it's the least compressible stage without changing the model or output length.

drills.q: Why does generation dominate the latency budget, and what levers actually exist to control it?
drills.a: Driven by output token count and model size, mostly outside retrieval's control. Levers: smaller/faster model where quality allows, capping/guiding output length, and streaming the first token to hide total latency from perceived UX (though total time-to-completion is unchanged).

drills.q: Explain the cascade retrieval pattern and why it's structured cheap-wide then expensive-narrow.
drills.a: Stage 1 (hybrid ANN, top 50-150) optimizes recall cheaply since ANN cost is roughly flat regardless of top-k. Stage 2 (cross-encoder rerank, top 3-20) optimizes precision but its cost scales linearly with candidate count, so it can only be run over the already-shrunk stage-1 output, not the whole corpus.

drills.q: Where does an extra point of recall stop being worth buying?
drills.a: Once the correct answer is already reliably inside the narrower set the reranker/generator will use -- additional recall past that point costs reranker latency and generation context tokens without changing the outcome, and can even hurt via lost-in-the-middle effects. Find the point by sweeping top-k against a recall@k eval and watching where the curve flattens.

drills.q: Why don't retrieval-quality techniques (hybrid, contextual retrieval, reranking, reformulation) stack additively?
drills.a: They partially overlap in which failures they fix -- rerank-over-hybrid often matches rerank-over-dense-only, meaning the reranker's gain subsumes much of the hybrid leg's contribution once both are in the pipeline. Precision returns flatten while each added stage's latency cost keeps accumulating linearly.

drills.q: A PM asks for "the highest possible retrieval accuracy" with no latency or cost budget. How do you respond?
drills.a: Push back constructively: every accuracy gain trades against latency/cost, so "highest possible" isn't an engineering target. Propose naming a concrete ceiling, build the budget against it, and show what accuracy that ceiling buys -- and note that even unlimited spend has a quality ceiling via lost-in-the-middle effects from excessive context.

drills.q: Retrieval meets its 2-second latency target and passes offline eval, but online task-completion hasn't improved after three successive retrieval-quality changes. What do you do?
drills.a: Stop shipping further retrieval-side changes on faith and instrument where the pipeline actually fails -- sample failed interactions and check whether the bottleneck is upstream (retrieval missing content), midstream (bad reranking), or downstream (generation failing to use good context, e.g. lost-in-the-middle). The likely hypothesis given three non-moving retrieval changes is that the bottleneck moved downstream of retrieval.

drills.q: A teammate says "just retrieve more chunks and pass them all to the LLM -- more context can only help." What's wrong with this, and how would you convince them otherwise?
drills.a: More chunks cost reranker latency/dilution, more input tokens, and past a threshold measurably hurt quality via lost-in-the-middle effects -- attention degrades on information buried in a long context. Convince with data: run the eval at increasing top-k/context sizes and show where the accuracy curve flattens or reverses, rather than just restating the mechanism.
